sentences.text: First-time founders
Considerations for a founder starting a company for the first time: what is hard, what to read and where to apply.
You are starting a company for the first time, so the vocabulary, the paperwork and the order of decisions are all new at once.
Nothing on this page assumes that you have raised money, signed a term sheet or read a cap table before.
Reading the documents of a first raise
A SAFE, a convertible note, a term sheet and a cap table each use their own terms, and the articles on them include questions to bring to your own counsel.
Choosing a route to money
Money can come from customers, grants, loans, investment or crowdfunding, and each route asks something different of the company and of you.
Recognizing how a company can end
Selling a company, selling its assets, an acqui-hire and a wind-down are four different events, with different votes, filings and records.
Paying the first helpers
Early founders pay first helpers by fixed fee, wages, deferred pay or shares, and each choice carries its own risk.
WE is a digital incubator for SaaS companies.
WE makes no promise of funding.
If this is your first company, the program's own description of a good fit is on the page about who the program is for.
Technical founders
Considerations for a founder who can build the product: the work that is not code, what to read and where to apply.
You can build the product yourself, so the open questions are mostly the ones that code does not answer.
Those are how customers pay, who owns what you have built and how the work gets funded.
Counting your own hours as a cost
Customer-funded growth competes with building for a technical founder's hours, because selling, support and billing all take time that the product does not get.
Writing down what a pilot is testing
A pilot exists to test a specific assumption, so the success criteria are worth writing into the agreement before it starts.
Checking who owns what you have built
Work built for a client is not automatically yours because you wrote it, so ownership is the first thing to check before turning client work into a product.
Testing whether a grant fits the work
Public grants pay for research and development, so the test is whether the project you would propose counts as research and development of the kind an agency's topic asks for.
WE is a digital incubator for SaaS companies.
WE steers the team and manages its subcontractors.
If you build the product yourself, the program's own description of a good fit is on the page about who the program is for.
Non-technical founders
Considerations for a founder who does not write code: what to check before you buy or build, what to read and where to apply.
You do not write code, so building a SaaS product means relying on other people's work and judging it without doing it yourself.
This page points to reading about staffing, ownership and money that makes that judgment easier to form.
Choosing how to staff the product work
Staffing product work is a choice among freelancers, an agency and a dedicated team, and the research brief on it sets out criteria for comparing them.
Checking a product before you buy it
Before buying a small software product, the first check is whether the seller owns the code.
Working out burn and runway
Runway is arithmetic, and the article on it shows what happens when one number changes and what the arithmetic hides.
Knowing what the rules say about investors
Founders talk about angels, micro-funds and funds as different investors, but US securities rules ask one legal question behind those labels.
WE is a digital incubator for SaaS companies, with dedicated offshore team seats steered by WE.
If you do not write code yourself, the program's own description of a good fit is on the page about who the program is for.
Solo founders
Considerations for a founder working alone: how to fund the work, who else to pay and what to read before you apply.
You are the only founder, so every decision, every task and every risk lands on one person.
This page points to reading about funding the work, paying first helpers and keeping the company running when you cannot.
Keeping prepaid service running
When customers prepay and you are the only person running the company, the contract needs to say what happens if you cannot deliver.
Keeping burn and runway in view
Burn and runway are worked from a few numbers, and the article includes a routine for keeping them in front of the person who decides.
Giving a side project a legal home
A side project starts to need a legal home, a bank account and written agreements at identifiable triggers, such as when other people use it or money changes hands.
Putting arrangements with helpers in writing
Whichever way a first helper is paid, the article includes a short list of items to put in writing: who the parties are, what is being done, what is paid and who owns the work.
WE is a digital incubator for SaaS companies.
WE offers dedicated offshore team seats.
If you are the only founder, the program's own description of a good fit is on the page about who the program is for.
Corporate innovators
Considerations for a person building a product out of an employer: who owns the work, what the agreements say and what to settle first.
You work for an employer and have a product idea that came out of that work, or sits close to it.
Who owns what you have made, what your agreement says and what your employer thinks are questions to settle before anything else.
Knowing who owns what you have made
Ownership comes from three layers: statute, your employment agreement and the facts of how the work was made.
Reading your own agreement
Statute is the floor and your contract may add to it, so every document you signed, including the ones you have not read since, goes to your lawyer.
Telling an employer-backed spin-out from a departure
An employer-backed spin-out is a negotiation between two parties who both want it, while a departure with an idea starts from interests that are not aligned.
Selling to a larger organization
If your first customer is a large organization, expect more steps, such as procurement review, security questions and legal review.

Student founders
Considerations for a founder who is still a student: who has a claim on the work, when a project needs a legal home and what to read.
You are building a product while you are still a student, so your school, your coursework and your own project may all touch the same work.
This page points to reading about who has a claim on a project, about grants and about when a side project needs a legal home.
Checking your school's claim on the work
Universities publish rules about who owns what students and researchers create, and one school's policy may be broader, narrower or different from another's.
Handling the first payment
The first payment turns a hobby into something an accountant and a tax authority may care about, so the article asks where the money goes and how it is recorded.
Testing a grant against a student project
SBIR and STTR awards go to for-profit companies, so a student project would have to be set up as one before it applies.

Second-career founders
Considerations for a founder moving into software from another career: starting points, client work and what to ask before joining.
You are moving into building a SaaS product from another line of work, and you may bring deep knowledge of one field more than of software.
This page points to reading about starting from a skill or a lived problem, about client work and about joining an early company.
Choosing a starting point
Founders begin from an idea, a skill or a problem they have lived, and the article sets the three side by side.
Turning service work into a product
A service business that turns repeated client work into a product has to check who owns what it has built, what client data it holds and how it prices.
Weighing an offer from an early company
The word founding describes several different arrangements, so the article suggests asking the person making the offer which one they mean and getting the answer in writing.
WE is a digital incubator for SaaS companies.
WE is fully remote.
If you are changing careers, the program's own description of a good fit is on the page about who the program is for.
Global and remote founders
Considerations for a founder who works from outside the United States or with a remote team: what changes and what to ask first.
You work from outside the United States, or your team is spread across countries and time zones.
This page points to reading on what US rules say about companies formed elsewhere and on the questions that location raises for pay, tax and work.
US rules for a company formed elsewhere
As the rule is written, Regulation Crowdfunding does not reach a company formed outside the United States, and only counsel can say what another structure would change.
Working across countries
Working from one country for a company formed in another raises employment, tax and sometimes immigration questions.
Choosing a payment route
One question to settle is which payroll or payment route the company will use and who handles social contributions and withholding.
Settling how a remote team works
Time zones, holidays and working hours are worth settling in writing, and the article points to what a written rhythm for a remote team covers.
